title: Double the bank levy
headline: Double the bank levy. Static, on HMRC’s 2024-25 receipts: about £1.3bn.
description: The bank levy is a charge on the balance sheets of the largest banks, created after the 2008 crisis. Its rate was halved in steps between 2015 and 2021, and receipts fell from £3.0 billion in 2016-17 to £1.3 billion in 2024-25. This card doubles the levy at HMRC’s 2024-25 receipts, so it raises what the levy raises today, grown with the OBR’s onshore corporation tax forecast. It is static: banks would shrink the chargeable balance sheet as they did when the rate fell. The bank surcharge, on profits, has its own card.

baselinePolicy.text: Bank levy receipts were £1.3 billion in 2024-25, down from £3.0 billion in 2016-17 as the rate was cut from 0.21% to 0.10% of chargeable equity and liabilities; the bank surcharge raised a further £1.0 billion.
alreadyIncludes: Corporation tax main rate 25% (Rates and allowances: Corporation Tax).

terms.label: Bank levy receipts in 2024-25: a second levy of the same size

rawSource.note: Static arithmetic: doubling the levy adds today’s receipts once more, grown with the OBR’s onshore corporation tax receipts from 2024-25. HMRC publishes the receipts to £0.1 billion, so the base is rounded to within about 10%.

caveats: Static. Banks shrink the chargeable balance sheet when the levy rises, and shift it abroad; receipts fell from £3.0bn to £1.3bn as the rate was halved, a fall that is more than the rate alone explains. Nobody has certified this number.

The levy falls on balance sheets and the surcharge on profits; they are separate taxes and this card leaves the surcharge where it is. HMRC publishes receipts to £0.1 billion; the 2026 edition of the statistics, due in late September 2026, would update the base.
Only banks and building societies with chargeable equity and liabilities above £20 billion pay, so the change falls on a few large groups.

considerations.text: Receipts fell from £3.0bn in 2016-17 to £1.3bn in 2024-25 while the rate was cut from 0.21% to 0.10%, a fall of more than half for a rate cut of a little over half: banks also trimmed the liabilities the levy reaches. A doubling would recover part of that, not all of it.

A charge on the largest banks’ balance sheets is borne by their shareholders, their customers through wider margins, or their staff, in shares nobody has measured; the OBR treats bank taxes as business taxes.

interactions.text: The two bank taxes stack: the surcharge on profits, the levy on balance sheets. Together they raise about £2.3bn today.
